info.name: Moments & Memories
info.description:
Every endpoint the product exposes, in the order you would exercise them.

Three realms, and they do not share credentials:
  • Mobile API  — /api/v1/*        Bearer {{token}}        (a customer)
  • Admin panel — /admin/v1/*      Bearer {{adminToken}}   (staff, 2FA)
  • Health      — /health          no auth

Pick an environment: "M&M — local" (http://127.0.0.1:3000) or "M&M — production" (https://api.72-61-173-62.sslip.io). In production the Admin panel folder answers 404 by design — nginx serves /api/v1/admin/ to nobody outside the server — and GET /vaults/debug/row-counts answers 404 too.

Tokens are captured automatically by the Tests script on each sign-in request, so run them top to bottom and nothing needs copying by hand.

Sign-in codes are SHA-256 in the database and cannot be read back. Either take the code from the inbox, or run:  npm run dev:code -- <email>

request.description: No auth, and deliberately so: a guard here would make every container fail its health check and roll the deploy back.
Readiness: this one touches the database. Use it to confirm the pool is actually up before blaming an endpoint.

Always 202, for any address.

That is the whole point: a 404 for unknown addresses would turn this into a way to ask the server whether somebody has an account here. Creating an account and signing in are the same request — there is no separate sign-up.

Set the `code` variable first.

One flat 401 for every failure — wrong code, expired code, too many attempts, no code at all. Distinguishing them would tell an attacker which part of the guess was right.

The token in the response is the only time that value exists outside your client; the database keeps its SHA-256 and nothing else. This script captures it into {{token}}.

exec: console.log('isNewAccount:', b.isNewAccount, '| expires in days:', b.expiresInDays);

The first endpoint that needs an actor. If this works, the whole chain works: bearer token → app_resolve_session → ActorContext → SET LOCAL app.user_id → sixty row-level policies.

type: personal | shared | legacy

Two writes in one transaction — the vault and the owner's membership row — so a vault with no members cannot exist.
Proof that the boundary belongs to the database rather than to a handler: the counts are what THIS actor can see, not what the tables hold.

body.raw:
{
  "title": "Aaji at the wedding",
  "note": "She wore the green sari.",
  "occurredAt": "1974-03-14T00:00:00Z",
  "occurredPrecision": "year",
  "occasion": "wedding",
  "clientId": "{{$guid}}"
}

request.description:
occurredAt is when it HAPPENED, not when it was uploaded — defaulting it to now is how a scanned 1974 photograph ends up filed under the Tuesday somebody digitised it.

occurredPrecision: exact | day | month | year | decade

clientId is the device's own id and makes a retry idempotent. {{$guid}} generates a fresh one; paste a fixed value instead to watch deduplicated flip to true.
Keyset pagination, not offset: an offset shifts under you when somebody adds a memory mid-scroll, and this timeline is appended to constantly. Pass nextBefore back as `before`.
Paging. `before` is an occurredAt instant: pass the oldest occurredAt from the previous page to get the page after it. The example returns the 1974 memory created above.

Returns a URL you PUT the file to DIRECTLY. The bytes never pass through this server.

`bytes` must match the file exactly — ContentLength is signed into the URL, so R2 rejects a body of a different size. kind: image | video | audio.

The quota is checked here, before a byte moves.

exec: console.log('PUT the file to the url in uploadUrl, then run Complete.');

request.description:
Body → binary → select your file. It must be the SAME file whose size you declared, or R2 refuses the signature.

Note there is no Authorization header: the signature in the URL is the credential, which is the whole reason this can go straight to Cloudflare.

The server HEADs the object and records the size IT reports, not the one you declared.

409 means the object is not in the bucket — you skipped the PUT, or it failed.
413 means the object is bigger than the upload was opened for.

A signed GET, 300 seconds. That TTL is the bound on how long a revoked share can still be opened, which is why it is capped at 900 in the schema rather than left to taste.

Open the url in a browser to see the file. Strip the query string and it fails — the bucket is private.

body.raw:
{
  "title": "For your eighteenth",
  "note": "You were asleep on my shoulder when I wrote this.",
  "unlockKind": "datetime",
  "unlockAt": "2044-03-01T09:00:00Z",
  "unlockTimezone": "Asia/Kolkata"
}

request.description:
Creates a DRAFT. unlockAt is when it opens; unlockTimezone is the zone the sender meant, kept separately so a message for a daughter in Pune scheduled from London does not arrive at 03:00 her time.

unlockKind: datetime | milestone | manual

unlockKind is datetime (needs unlockAt), manual (sealed but never scheduled — released by hand), or milestone (needs milestoneMemberId, a members.id). No endpoint creates members yet, so milestone cannot be exercised from here.

Returns only the recipient's id. No credential is handed out — not even to the sender.

The token that opens the capsule is minted by the worker at delivery and travels only in the message that delivers it. A sender holding one could open the capsule first and become "the first opening".

To try the /open requests locally: run the worker (npm run worker:dev), let it deliver, and paste the token from its `[dev] ... link:` log line into the accessToken collection variable.
Idempotent — the primary key makes a retry a no-op. Send twice and watch added drop to 0 while total stays the same.

A draft is freely editable: title, note, unlockAt, unlockTimezone. Send only what changes; null clears title, note or unlockTimezone.

After the seal, the same request works only inside the 15-minute grace window (see the request after the seal).

A recipient needs an email or a phone. preferredChannel is push, email, sms or whatsapp, and the matching field is required: sms and whatsapp need phone, email needs email.

Added here only to be removed by the next request.
Only while the capsule is a draft. Once sealed, its recipients are settled: 409.

Seals the capsule AND schedules its delivery in ONE transaction. A capsule sealed without a job is a promise nothing will ever keep.

400 no recipients · 400 unlock time already passed · 409 already sealed · 403 not the owner

scheduled:false means it was sealed but has no date yet (milestone or manual).

Inside the 15-minute grace window this succeeds. After it, capsule_freeze() raises 23514 and you get 400.

The freeze is a database trigger, not a check in the handler — it holds for every writer, including an admin tool or a migration script.
The capsule with its recipients and memories. The access token is NOT here, in any form.
state filters by one of: draft, sealed, delivering, delivered, opened, cancelled, failed.

NO Authorization header — that is the point. The recipient may have been eleven when this was written and may have no account.

Before delivery this is 404. A wrong token is the same flat 404, so a bad token learns nothing.

Works once the worker has delivered the capsule. The token is the last path segment of the link in the delivery message; locally, the worker logs it as `[dev] ... link: <OPEN_LINK_BASE_URL>/<token>`. Copy that token into the accessToken collection variable.

Each delivery attempt mints a new token and revokes the previous one, so use the token from the latest log line.

Records the FIRST opening only — refresh and firstOpenedAt does not move.
The reply the sender may never read. Goes through app_post_reply(), which refuses any capsule not delivered or opened.

Withdraw the promise. Allowed after sealing, unlike editing: a promise you may silently rewrite is not a promise, but a person must always be able to stop something being sent.

The job is NOT deleted — the worker completes it without sending, keeping the record that something was scheduled and then withdrawn.
Revokes every session except the one making the request. Run this BEFORE sign-out, or you will have nothing left to call it with.
After this, every request above returns 401 until you sign in again.

Also always 202, so this cannot be used to enumerate staff.

The address must already exist in admin_users — there is no self-signup for staff, by design.

Factor one. The mfaToken it returns can do exactly ONE thing — present a TOTP code. It reaches no other admin route.

On a first sign-in the response also carries `enrolment`, containing the TOTP secret and otpauth URI. It is shown once and is never recoverable: re-enrolment is refused once a secret exists, because otherwise anybody holding a first-factor token could replace the second factor with one of their own.

exec: console.log('Add the otpauth URI to your authenticator app.');

request.description:
Factor two. Note the Authorization header carries the mfaToken, not a session.

Set `totp` to the six digits from your authenticator. The admin session lasts 8 hours, not the 30 days a customer gets.

Everything the console's home screen draws. Run `npm run seed:dev` first or the numbers are all zero.

Worth noticing what is NOT here: no capsule contents. The console connects as mm_admin, which has a column-level grant letting it count capsules and read unlock_at, but no SELECT on sender_note at all. Operations can see that a capsule exists without reading what somebody wrote to their daughter.
The realms do not share credentials. A customer session must never open a staff door, and this proves it.
